To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

HTLV-I associated myelopathy/tropic spastic parapareis (HAM/TSp) is a sexually acquired disease that is clinically characterized by a more severe and progressive course than spastic paraparaparesis of unknown etiology (SPOneg).
HAM/TSP is a sexually transmitted disease, and that it can be clinically discriminated from SPOneg prior to serological tests.
HTLV-I associated myelopathy/tropic spastic parapareis (HAM/Tsp) and HTLV negative spastic parapeis of obscure origin(Spon) are clinically similar diseases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the clinical features of HAM/TSP and SPOneg in order to find out whether they can be differentiated prior to serological tests.
the study of the HTLV-I infection and its association with neurological diseases.
the identification of clinical and laboratory markers that can help to differentiate HAM/TSP from SPOneg, and with the identification of risk factors for HAM/TSP.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

HAM/TSP can only be diagnosed with certainty after the demonstration of the presence of antibodies against HTLV-I, and that the only risk factor for infection significantly associated with the disease in our study was a previous history of STD.

the presence of bladder dysfunction, constipation or penile impotence and an intrathecal synthesis are more frequent in HTLV-I infected SPO patients, and a history of sexually transmitted disease is the most important risk factor for HTVL-I infection.
HAM/TSP and SPOneg are two distinct entities, with different risk factors and different clinical and paraclinical characteristics.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
, in our experience, the clinical picture of HAM/TSP is not different from that of SPO, but the disease is more severe and progresses faster in HTLV-I positive patients.
the diagnosis of HAM/TSP can be made in the majority of patients with a high level of confidence by means of a careful clinical evaluation.
HAM/TSP can be differentiated from HTLV-I negative SPOneg in a high percentage of cases by the presence of bladder and sexual disturbances and the presence of widespread pyramidal findings.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the clinical picture in HTLV-I infected SPO patients tends to be more severe and progressive, and that the presence of bladder dysfunction and widespread pyramidal tract signs are the best predictors of HTLV-I infection.

, in the absence of a serological test, the presence of motor and bladder dysfunction at the beginning of the illness, and of pyramidal signs during the whole course, are the most important clinical clues to the diagnosis of HAM/TSP.

, in our experience, the presence of bladder dysfunction, constipation or penile impotence and the presence of widespread pyramidal tract signs are the most useful clinical findings for discriminating HTLV-I positive from HTLV-I negative patients.
